content: Clostridium perfringens is a bacterium that is a leading cause of foodborne illness in the United States. It is estimated that nearly 1 million cases of food poisoning caused by this bacterium occur annually in the country. C. perfringens has the ability to form spores, which are structures with protective coatings that allow the bacteria to survive in harsh conditions. When a person consumes food contaminated with C. perfringens, the bacteria can produce a toxin in the intestines. This toxin is responsible for causing symptoms such as diarrhea. Foods that are most commonly associated with C. perfringens food poisoning are those prepared in large quantities and held at unsafe temperatures, specifically between 40°F and 140°F. Examples of such foods include poultry (like turkey and chicken), meats (such as beef and pork), and gravy. Outbreaks of C. perfringens food poisoning frequently occur in environments where food is prepared and served to large groups of people, and where maintaining proper food temperatures can be challenging. These settings include hospitals, school cafeterias, prisons, nursing homes, and large events with catered meals. The majority of outbreaks tend to occur during the months of November and December. Many of these outbreaks have been linked to traditional holiday foods, such as turkey and roast beef.
